title: Firecracker Smoke Is Making Eyes Burn After Diwali: What Eye Doctors Advise
excerpt: Ophthalmologists explain why Diwali smoke burns even bystanders' eyes, the relief steps that work, and the first-aid sequence that matters if a cracker actually injures an eye.
body:
• Firecracker smoke carries fine particles, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and metal salts that irritate the conjunctiva and destabilise the tear film, causing burning, redness and watering even in people who burst no crackers.
  • For smoke irritation: use preservative-free lubricating drops, apply a cool compress, do not rub, and switch from contact lenses to glasses for a few days.
  • For a cracker injury: do not rub or try to remove an embedded particle, rinse dust or ash with clean water for 10 to 15 minutes, cover the eye lightly with no pressure, and go to an eye specialist or emergency department immediately.
  • See a doctor the same day if pain worsens, light hurts, vision blurs, discharge appears, or redness lasts beyond 24 to 48 hours.

You do not have to burst a single cracker to wake up after Diwali with red, burning, watery eyes. Firecracker smoke travels across neighbourhoods and hangs in the air for hours, exposing people indoors as well, according to ophthalmologists quoted by OnlyMyHealth in a guide medically reviewed by Dr Shibal Bhartiya, clinical director of ophthalmology at Marengo Asia Hospitals, Gurugram.

Why the smoke burns

Firecracker smoke contains fine particulate matter, gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, and metal salts — barium, strontium, copper and aluminium — used to produce colours. On contact, these pollutants irritate the conjunctiva, the thin membrane covering the white of the eye, and disturb the tear film that keeps the eye surface moist. An unstable tear film produces burning, redness, a gritty feeling and watering, which is the eye's attempt to flush the irritants out.

Some people are hit faster and harder. Pollution further disrupts the already unstable tear film of people with dry eye disease. Allergy sufferers get more redness, itching and watering. Contact lens users face a specific risk: fine particles can lodge under a lens against the cornea, raising the risk of corneal abrasions and infection. Children and older adults tend to develop symptoms sooner, and people with conditions such as glaucoma should keep taking their prescribed drops without interruption — pollution irritation is not a reason to stop them.

What to do for smoke irritation

For irritation without an injury, the doctors' advice is simple. Use preservative-free artificial tears to restore moisture and flush out irritants, and rest a clean, cool cloth over closed eyelids for a few minutes. Do not rub: rubbing worsens inflammation and can damage the corneal surface. Wash your face gently, keep windows and doors closed while smoke levels are high, wear wraparound glasses outdoors, and do not self-prescribe antibiotic or steroid drops, which can cause complications and delay proper treatment.

First aid for an actual eye injury

Burns and flying debris are a different emergency from smoke irritation. Dr Sripriya P, a consultant ophthalmologist at Dr Agarwals Eye Hospital in Bengaluru, told TezzBuzz that a cracker bursting near the face can scratch the cornea, cloud the lens or, in the worst cases, rupture the eyeball — and that the first minutes decide the outcome. Her sequence: stop anyone rubbing the eye; rinse dust, ash or a chemical splash with clean, cool water for 10 to 15 minutes; never try to pull out an embedded particle with fingers, tissue, cotton buds or tweezers; cover the eye gently with a clean shield or light dressing with nothing pressing on the eyeball; and get to an eye specialist or emergency department at once rather than waiting to see if it settles overnight. The PGIMER Chandigarh ophthalmology department's Diwali advisory gives the same instruction: do not rub, cover lightly, and reach an ophthalmologist immediately.

Prevention for the remaining festive days

Wear polycarbonate safety glasses or protective goggles when lighting or watching crackers — ordinary spectacles are not a substitute. Keep at least five metres away once a cracker is lit, and do not set off rockets near curtained windows or in narrow lanes where they can bounce back. Mild smoke irritation should improve within 24 to 48 hours once exposure stops; worsening pain, sensitivity to light, blurred or reduced vision, thick discharge, or redness that persists despite lubricating drops all need an ophthalmologist, because they can signal a corneal scratch, an infection or a flare-up of an existing condition.
